hook.text: A point mutation changes just one base in the DNA. One letter swap can rewrite the whole message.

buildup.text: A missense mutation swaps one amino acid. A nonsense mutation creates an early stop signal.

discovery.text: Silent mutations change the DNA letter but not the amino acid, thanks to code redundancy.

twist.text: Sickle cell disease comes from a single point mutation—A to T—in the hemoglobin gene.

climax.text: One base out of 3.2 billion changed, and it reshapes red blood cells into crescents.

punchline.text: One letter. One protein. One disease.

quiz.question: What does a nonsense mutation do?
options: Creates an early stop signal in the protein
Swaps one amino acid for another
Has no effect on the protein

details.summary: Point mutations change a single nucleotide base in the DNA sequence. They can be silent with no protein change, missense producing a different amino acid, or nonsense creating a premature stop codon. Sickle cell disease results from just one point mutation.
details.whyItMatters: A single base change can have effects ranging from invisible to lethal. Point mutations are the most common type of genetic variation and the primary source of new alleles driving evolution and causing genetic disease.
takeaways: Silent mutations change a codon but not the amino acid it encodes
Missense mutations swap one amino acid for another in the protein
Nonsense mutations create premature stop codons that truncate proteins

faq.question: How does one base change cause sickle cell disease?
faq.answer: A single A-to-T substitution changes one amino acid in hemoglobin from glutamic acid to valine. This causes hemoglobin molecules to stick together under low oxygen, distorting red blood cells into rigid sickle shapes that block blood vessels.

faq.question: Why are some point mutations silent?
faq.answer: The genetic code is redundant, with multiple codons encoding the same amino acid. A base change in the third position of a codon often specifies the same amino acid, producing no change in the protein. These silent mutations accumulate without effect.
